title: Radical Equations
short: Isolate the root, raise both sides to a power, and check.
trouble: Students square each term separately, or skip checking for extraneous solutions.

blocks.html: To solve an equation with a root, undo the root by raising both sides to a power, the inverse step you know from nth Roots and Simplifying and Rationalizing Radicals. Squaring is powerful, but it can create answers that aren't real solutions, so checking is part of the method.

Isolate the radical. Raise both sides to the index (square for $\sqrt{\ }$, cube for $\sqrt[3]{\ }$). Solve. Then check every answer in the original equation and throw out any that fail (extraneous solutions).

If $a = b$ then $a^2 = b^2$, but the reverse is false: $a^2 = b^2$ also holds when $a = -b$. So squaring adds the solutions of a second equation, the one with the opposite sign. A square root is never negative, so any answer that would make a square root equal a negative number belongs to that other equation and must be rejected. Cubing doesn't have this problem, because $a^3 = b^3$ only when $a = b$.

blocks.name: graph
blocks.cap: $f(x) = \sqrt{x + 3}$ and $g(x) = x + 1$ meet only at $x = 1$. Squaring also produces $x = -2$, which is where $h(x) = -\sqrt{x + 3}$ (dashed) meets the line: a solution of a different equation.

blocks.title: An extraneous solution
steps: Check $x = -2$: $\sqrt{1} = 1$ but $-2 + 1 = -1$. Fails, so it is extraneous.

blocks.html: Squaring term by term. $(x + 1)^2$ is $x^2 + 2x + 1$, not $x^2 + 1$, and you can't square $\sqrt{x - 2} + 4$ by squaring each piece. Isolate the root first, then square whole sides. And always check: skipping the check is how extraneous answers sneak in.
